title: Tokyo Breaks New Ground as Billboard Honors the Executives Shaping Global Music
summary: For the first time, the Billboard Global Power Players awards touched down in Asia, transforming a Tokyo hotel ballroom into a crossroads of the international music business. The June 12 ceremony, part of MUSIC AWARDS JAPAN 2026 WEEK, honored executives who are reshaping how music travels across borders—and it did so with a distinctly Japanese flair. Bilingual host mikako guided the audience through tributes in English and Japanese, while Billboard CEO Mike Van noted the event’s expansion across 15 international editions. The night’s three special awards spotlighted individuals who have turned local talent into global phenomena. Marlene Tsuchii of CAA received the Artist Advocate Award, presented by dancer Miyu, who credited Tsuchii with making her the first Japanese dancer signed to the agency. Tsuchii, who has spent nearly 25 years at CAA, reflected on her work bridging Japanese acts like YOASOBI and BABYMETAL to international markets. “I feel an inherent responsibility to expand the reach of Japanese artists,” she said, citing her family roots in Tokyo and Hiroshima. The Global Growth Award went to Avex Inc. Music Group CEO Katsumi Kuroiwa and Avex Music Group USA CEO Brandon Silverstein, recognized for their innovative publishing partnership with Bruno Mars. Kuroiwa humbly noted that Avex began as a small record rental shop and succeeded globally only through collaboration. The Impact Award honored Rachel Newman, Co-Head of Music at Apple Music, who has driven the platform’s growth across 160 countries. “I’ve always believed that music is that magical something that can change us,” she said. The ceremony concluded with a forward-looking speech by CEIPA Chairman Shunsuke Muramatsu, who called the event “a dream that many in the Japanese music industry have held for many years” and emphasized the need for persistence: “When we look back five or ten years from now, I want us to be able to say that this is where it all began.”
why_it_matters: This event shows that the international music industry is no longer centered only in the U.S. or Europe; Asia, and especially Japan, is becoming a major player. For a teenager, understanding these shifts can open eyes to global careers in creative fields and to the idea that the music you stream on your phone is shaped by people working behind the scenes across continents.

questions.correct_answer: That this is where it all began

background_read: Billboard (the American music magazine founded in 1894, famous for its record charts like the Hot 100) publishes international editions covering music trends around the world and honors industry leaders through its Power Players events.
CAA (Creative Artists Agency, one of the largest talent agencies globally) represents athletes, actors, and musicians, and has played a key role in bringing Japanese acts to international stages.

YOASOBI (a Japanese music duo that transforms short stories into songs) and BABYMETAL (a genre-blending “kawaii metal” band) are two of the Japanese artists who have built substantial fanbases outside Japan, showing the growing global taste for J-pop.

Avex Inc. (a major Japanese entertainment company that started as a small record rental shop in 1988) now manages and publishes music worldwide, including partnerships with Western superstars like Bruno Mars.

Apple Music, launched in 2015, streams music in over 160 countries and has become a vital platform for promoting both local and international artists, helping shape what millions of listeners hear every day.

perspectives.description: The awards celebrate individuals who bring Japanese music to global audiences, creating economic and cultural opportunities for artists like YOASOBI and BABYMETAL, and showing that talent from any country can become a worldwide sensation with the right support.

As big global companies and agencies work to export local music, there is a risk that artists must change their style to fit international tastes, which could water down the unique qualities of national music scenes and prioritize profit over authenticity.

The shift of such a ceremony to Tokyo reflects deeper economic and demographic trends: Asia’s large and young streaming audience is driving music revenue growth, and western companies are eager to tap into that market through partnerships and local editions.

If the Japanese music industry continues to invest in international connections and artist development, we might see more Japanese acts headlining global festivals or topping worldwide charts — and similar recognition events could start popping up in other cities like Seoul or Mumbai.
